text: When should you choose an abstract class over an interface?
choices: Whenever the subclasses will be numerous, since interfaces do not scale past a few implementers.
Whenever you need to provide any shared behaviour, since interfaces cannot have bodies.
When the implementations genuinely share state and code and are honestly kinds of one thing, and you control them all.
Whenever you want to forbid instantiation, which an interface cannot do.
explanation: Since Java 8 gave interfaces default and static methods, the distinction narrowed to state and the single-superclass budget. An abstract class costs implementers their one inheritance slot; an interface costs them nothing they may need elsewhere. When unsure, choose the interface — it constrains less and composes with others, and Chapter 23 argues that the commitment inheritance requires is worth avoiding when you can.
